fatal_flaws.claim: §4 Runtime topology: '*/*' catch-all route → renderer, with 'Exact-hostname Custom Domains are how the other three surfaces carve themselves out of that wildcard'; verification deferred to 'before Phase 3'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Backwards. Cloudflare's own routing docs state: 'Routes can fetch() Custom Domains and take precedence if configured on the same hostname' — the documented example is a Custom Domain on app.example.com losing ingress to a Route at app.example.com/*. The Cloudflare-for-SaaS 'Workers as your fallback origin' page confirms the same model: with a wildcard */* route, 'that route pattern matches all traffic entering your zone, including traffic from custom hostnames', and the documented carve-out mechanism is adding *routes* (including routes with no Worker specified) — not Custom Domains. So as designed, app.mijnsaas.com and api.mijnsaas.com are served by the renderer, and mijnsaas.com's assets-only marketing Worker stops being assets-only (every marketing request becomes a billed renderer invocation, destroying the '0 invocations, free requests' claim). The ordering error is worse than the technical one: apps/api ships on a Custom Domain in Phase 1, and the doc defers verification to Phase 3.
fatal_flaws.correction: Bind all four surfaces as Routes, using specificity: `mijnsaas.com/*` and `www.mijnsaas.com/*` → marketing, `app.mijnsaas.com/*` → app, `api.mijnsaas.com/*` → api, `*/*` → renderer; each needs its own proxied DNS record (AAAA 100:: is fine). Alternatively keep Custom Domains and scope the renderer to `*.mijnsaas.com/*` until Phase 3, then add empty routes to exclude the app/api hostnames from `*/*`. Either way this must be proven on a real deployed zone in Phase 1, not staging-before-Phase-3 — and the assets-only-Worker billing behaviour must be re-confirmed when bound by Route rather than Custom Domain.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7 Phase 1: 'apps/api (Hono: Zod validation, direct-to-R2 media upload, Workflow dispatch)' — onboarding modal posts, API validates, Workflow runs the Claude chain. Only 'Regenerate' is paywalled.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The first generation is unauthenticated, unmetered and free to the caller, and it is the most expensive operation in the product. claude-opus-5 is $5/MTok in, $25/MTok out. Step 2 runs at effort:high with adaptive thinking (thinking tokens bill as output) and 128K max_tokens; step 3 adds two blog posts; step 4 fans out 5 translations. A realistic run is single-digit dollars of output tokens. ACV is €119,88 (~$130) minus Stripe fees. The design contains no Turnstile, no per-IP or per-session quota, no concurrency cap, no per-run token ceiling, no account-level Anthropic spend cap, and no kill switch — and Workflows' 50,000-instance concurrency plus 300 instances/sec creation rate means a script can spend thousands of dollars per hour against an API key with no cap. This is not a scaling worry; it is a day-one financial DoS on a public endpoint.
fatal_flaws.correction: Gate Workflow dispatch behind Turnstile + a server-issued onboarding token, a per-IP/per-fingerprint quota and a global concurrency cap (Durable Object counter or Queues). Put a hard per-run ceiling on spend using output_config.task_budget (beta task-budgets-2026-03-13, min 20,000 tokens) plus conservative max_tokens per step, and log usage per generation_run into D1. Set an org-level spend alert on the Anthropic key. Consider requiring the Stripe trial (card on file) before the FIRST generation, not just regeneration — that is a product-constraint conversation with the client, and it should be raised explicitly rather than discovered from a bill.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4 step 2: 'Claude: structure + copy in primary locale — client.messages.parse(), output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(SiteDocSchema), effort: "high" }, thinking: { type: "adaptive" }, streaming (large max_tokens)'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: client.messages.parse() does not stream and never did — the SDKs' parse(stream=...) argument was removed precisely because it never streamed. You cannot have both in one call. Since the design itself (correctly) requires streaming for large max_tokens, the parse() helper is the wrong entry point for exactly the call the whole architecture is built on. This is the single most-copied snippet in the doc and it 400s / silently drops streaming depending on SDK version.
fatal_flaws.correction: Use the streaming helper with the same structured-output config: `const stream = client.messages.stream({ model: 'claude-opus-5', max_tokens: 64000, thinking: { type: 'adaptive' }, output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(SiteDocSchema), effort: 'high' }, messages: [...] }); const msg = await stream.finalMessage();` then run SiteDocSchema.safeParse() on the JSON yourself. Keep messages.parse() only for the small non-streaming calls (translations at effort:low), where it is genuinely the better helper.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5: 'One SiteDocSchema (Zod v4) is simultaneously (a) the DB/R2 document shape, (b) the renderer's input type, (c) the editor's form model, and (d) the Anthropic structured-output format via zodOutputFormat. One definition, four consumers — the AI physically cannot emit something the renderer can't draw.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two hard limits break this. (1) Structured-output JSON schemas do not support recursive schemas. The doc describes SiteDoc as a 'page tree' and 'section list' — the natural renderer/editor shape (sections containing sections, nav with children, rich-text nodes) is recursive, and that shape cannot be sent as an output format at all. (2) Numerical and string constraints (minimum/maximum, minLength/maxLength, pattern) are NOT supported and are stripped by the Python/TS SDKs before the request, then validated client-side. So every meta-title length limit, hex-colour pattern, slug format and enum-of-real-section-types constraint you rely on is a post-hoc validation failure discovered after you have paid full price for a 128K-token generation — and the Workflow has no repair or retry-with-errors step. The keystone claim is therefore false in both directions: the AI can emit documents the renderer cannot draw (semantically invalid but schema-valid), and the renderer's real type cannot be handed to the model.
fatal_flaws.correction: Split the contract explicitly: `SiteDocSchema` (renderer/editor/storage, recursive and constrained) and `SiteGenSchema` (flat, non-recursive, no numeric/string constraints, discriminated union of section types by literal enum) plus a pure `genToDoc()` adapter in packages/site-schema. Test that adapter as hard as the schema. Add a Workflow step that, on Zod failure, re-prompts once with the validation errors before failing the run, and record both attempts in generation_runs. Drop the 'physically cannot emit' claim — replace it with 'schema-valid by construction, semantically validated by genToDoc + a lint pass (contrast, required fields, section-type compatibility)'.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.3: 'KV lookup: host → { siteId, liveVersion, ... } (~1ms, edge-local)' and 'Because the Cache API key contains the version, publishing is just bump liveVersion in KV. No purge API call, no purge race, no stale-content window.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: ~1ms is the hot-key figure (Cloudflare documents hot-key cache hits at 500µs–10ms). A cold read walks nearest regional tier → central tier → central store. At 10,000 tenants across ~330 colos with a 50-visit/day long tail, the routing key is cold in most colos most of the time — the exact same long-tail problem the doc correctly diagnoses for R2 and then assumes away for KV. Separately, 'no stale-content window' is false as written: KV is eventually consistent with up to 60s global propagation, so different colos serve different liveVersion values concurrently after a publish (and can serve v(N) HTML referencing v(N+1)-only assets), and the design's own browser-facing `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` adds five more minutes. The predictable support ticket is 'I clicked publish and my site didn't change.'
fatal_flaws.correction: Say what it actually is: no purge *race* and no purge *quota*, with a bounded ≤60s propagation window. Coalesce the manifest so one KV read serves the whole site (it already does) and keep it small. Serve the editor's own 'view live site' link with a cache-busting version query so the owner sees the new version immediately. Drop browser max-age to ~60s with `stale-while-revalidate`, or keep 300s only on immutable versioned asset URLs. Consider fronting the manifest with a Durable Object or the Cache API for the colo-cold case, and measure cold-read p95 before quoting 1ms anywhere.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.1 scoring: Hybrid gets 5/5 on Cacheability and 5/5 on Cost/request, tying pure build→R2; §3.3 defers the Tiered-Cache miss path to 'when RUM shows it'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The doc is right that the Cache API is colo-local and does not participate in Tiered Cache — and that fact invalidates its own scoring. For a local bakery with 50 visits/day scattered across European colos, the steady-state Cache API hit rate is near zero, so the hybrid's real serving profile is 'an R2 read on nearly every request', not 5/5 cacheability. Meanwhile strategy 2 served from an R2 public custom domain rides the ordinary CDN path and gets Tiered Cache (and optionally Cache Reserve) for free. So the miss path the doc defers is not an optimisation — it is the thing that makes the scoring true, and it requires a second zone, i.e. a topology change, not a tuning knob. 'Ship the binding version first; add this when it's measurable' will not surface cleanly in RUM either: the signal is a modest TTFB tail on low-traffic tenants, which is exactly what you cannot see until you have thousands of them.
fatal_flaws.correction: Build the miss path as `fetch(r2PublicUrl, { cf: { cacheEverything: true, cacheTtl: 31536000 } })` from day one, with the R2 public custom domain on the second zone (correctly noted: it must sit outside the */* route). Keep the versioned Cache API entry as an L1 in front of it. Restate the scoring honestly: hybrid ties strategy 2 on cacheability only once the tiered miss path exists, and wins on editor round-trip and preview fidelity — which is still enough to win the comparison.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4: 'system prompt → component/section catalog → SiteDoc JSON schema → industry design tokens, all marked cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Wrong on economics and on layout. Economics: 1h-TTL cache writes cost 2× base input and need at least three requests sharing the prefix within the hour to break even (5-minute TTL: 1.25× write, break-even at two requests). Early-stage generation traffic arrives minutes-to-hours apart, so nearly every run pays a 2× write it never reads back. Layout: putting the per-industry design tokens *inside* the cached prefix fragments one cache namespace into 5–8 archetype namespaces, cutting the already-low hit rate by roughly the number of archetypes — the exact mistake the doc warns about one sentence earlier. Also note the design uses all four available cache_control breakpoints, leaving no room to add one later.
fatal_flaws.correction: Cache only the genuinely shared, high-volume prefix — system prompt → section catalog → SiteGen JSON schema — as ONE breakpoint on the default 5-minute TTL. Put industry tokens and tenant business data AFTER the last breakpoint (they are cheap and they are what varies). Assert `usage.cache_read_input_tokens > 0` in a test and alert if it is zero in production; Opus 5's minimum cacheable prefix is 512 tokens, so the catalog+schema will clear it easily, but a silent invalidator (unsorted JSON, a timestamp) will make you pay 1.25–2× for nothing. Move to ttl:'1h' only once measured generation cadence is faster than one per hour per archetype.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4: tenant sites at <slug>.mijnsaas.com, dashboard at app.mijnsaas.com, API at api.mijnsaas.com — one zone, one registrable domain.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Attacker-influenced content (AI-authored HTML, tenant-edited copy, tenant-uploaded media) shares a registrable domain with the authenticated dashboard and the API. mijnsaas.com is not on the Public Suffix List, so a tenant subdomain can set cookies scoped to `.mijnsaas.com` — cookie tossing and session fixation against app.mijnsaas.com — SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies are sent on navigations originating from tenant sites, and any 'is this same-site?' check in the API is not a security boundary. One stored-XSS on any of 10,000 tenant sites becomes a foothold against every logged-in dashboard session. This is the painful one-way door in the document: slugs get indexed, printed on business cards, and linked from Google Business Profiles, so you cannot move them later.
fatal_flaws.correction: Move the dashboard and API to a different registrable domain now (tenant sites keep mijnsaas.com, which is what the client constraint actually pins). Use `__Host-` prefixed session cookies, an explicit Origin allowlist on the API rather than same-site inference, and a strict CSP on the renderer with no inline script beyond the ~1 KB cookie banner. Serve tenant media from a third registrable domain with restricted content types. If keeping one domain is non-negotiable, a PSL submission for mijnsaas.com is the only real mitigation — and it takes months, so it has to start in Phase 1.

fatal_flaws.claim: §1: 'Hero video from R2 must be a compressed MP4/WebM ladder (or Cloudflare Stream) — a raw 20 MB MP4 destroys mobile CWV', combined with §7 Phase 1 'direct-to-R2 media upload' and a Workflow with no encoding step.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The design states the requirement and then never satisfies it. Onboarding accepts video uploads straight into R2; the Workflow's eight steps contain no transcode; Workers cannot transcode video. So the shipped behaviour is: a small business uploads a 150 MB portrait phone video from an iPhone and it becomes the full-screen hero. Every CWV and Lighthouse claim in the doc dies on that path, and Cloudflare Stream — the only realistic answer on this platform — is a separate paid product (per-minute stored + per-minute delivered) that appears in no cost table here.
fatal_flaws.correction: Pick one and put it in Phase 1: (a) restrict onboarding uploads to images, and source hero video exclusively from the Pexels/Unsplash step (already in the Workflow) with pre-vetted encodes; or (b) budget Cloudflare Stream, add an upload→Stream ingest step, and gate publish on encoding completion. Either way, enforce content-type and size limits at the presign step, and give the renderer a documented fallback (poster-only hero) for any tenant whose video is missing or still encoding.

fatal_flaws.claim: §6.11: 'Images: transformations are $0.50 per 1,000 unique transformations (5,000/mo free)... generate a fixed variant set at publish time, don't transform per request per breakpoint — that's an unbounded bill.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The pricing figure is correct, but the mitigation misunderstands the meter. Transformations are billed per unique (source image, options) combination **once per month**, not once ever. Generating a fixed variant set at publish time does not make the cost one-time — every variant that is still being served re-bills every month. At 10,000 tenants × ~20 images × 4 breakpoint variants that is ~800,000 unique transformations/month ≈ $400/month, recurring and growing linearly with tenant count, on ~€100k ARR.
fatal_flaws.correction: Transform once at publish and write the derivative back into R2 as a plain object (`media/{tenantId}/{hash}/{w}.avif`), then serve those objects directly — after the first month you pay R2 storage (~$0.015/GB-mo, free egress) instead of the transformation meter forever. Reserve /cdn-cgi/image/ for the publish-time pass only.

fatal_flaws.claim: §0: overriding the client's stated Workers+Pages constraint, justified by '@astrojs/cloudflare v13 (March 2026) dropped Pages support entirely and Astro 6 requires v13+. Choosing Pages would mean choosing an adapter that no longer supports it.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The adapter argument does not apply to the surface it is used on. The marketing site is `output: 'static'` — a static Astro build requires no Cloudflare adapter at all and deploys to Pages unchanged; the v13 Pages removal only affects SSR deployments. Every genuinely Workers-only feature cited (Workflows, Cron Triggers, Secrets Store, Containers) lives in the api/generator/renderer Workers, which nobody proposed putting on Pages. So the one hard client constraint the document overrides is overridden on a reason that does not hold for the one surface where Pages was ever in play. Minor knock-ons: the doc pins @astrojs/cloudflare v13 for a build that does not need it, and credits it with 'bindings behave the same in dev and prod' for a static build that has no bindings.
fatal_flaws.correction: Keep Workers Static Assets — it is the better call — but justify it correctly and get explicit client sign-off rather than asserting the override. The honest argument is: Cloudflare's own docs direct new projects to Workers, Pages is in maintenance, Workers Static Assets gives identical free static-asset billing, and one deployment primitive across five deployables beats two. Frame it to the client as 'Workers Static Assets is Pages' successor', flag it as a deviation from a stated non-negotiable, and drop the adapter from apps/marketing entirely.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.4 / §6.5: 'D1 = metadata + pointers only... Small rows, thousands of tenants ≈ tens of MB. Comfortably inside 10 GB forever.' / 'D1: 10 GB hard cap, single-writer, one query at a time. Metadata only.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Correct facts, wrong conclusion. The doc identifies single-writer/one-query-at-a-time and then answers a *throughput* question with a *size* answer. At 10,000 tenants the binding constraint is not 10 GB — it is that every publish, autosave metadata flush, Stripe webhook, custom-hostname status poll and generation_run row serialises through one writer on one database in one region. The doc even quotes Cloudflare's design philosophy ('ten databases, not one') and then designs one.
fatal_flaws.correction: Decide the shard key in Phase 1, while packages/db is a single Drizzle file: a stable tenant-hash or per-region D1 with a small routing table in KV. Keep genuinely global tables (slug registry, custom_hostnames) in one D1 and shard the per-tenant write-heavy ones. Resharding once 10,000 tenants are live is exactly the painful migration the doc is otherwise good at avoiding. Also confirm D1 location_hint is set to an EU region, and adopt the Sessions API bookmarks the doc already correctly flags.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4 Workflow steps 2–7, with the 6-simultaneous-connection limit called out only for the locale fan-out.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two unstated Workflows constraints bite here. A non-stream step.do() return value caps at 1 MiB — a 6-locale SiteDoc plus two blog posts can approach that, and returning materialised HTML between steps certainly exceeds it. Step timeouts cap at 30 minutes. And the 6-simultaneous-connection limit applies just as much to step 7's ~48 R2 puts as to step 4's translation calls, which is the only place the doc mentions it.
fatal_flaws.correction: Pass R2 keys between steps, never payloads. Make each locale its own step.do() so retries are per-locale rather than re-running the whole fan-out (and so a single failed translation does not cost you five more Claude calls). Chunk the 48 R2 writes to ≤6 in flight. Set explicit per-step retry policies and an explicit timeout on the Claude steps, and make every step idempotent — they will be retried.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.2/§3.5: multilingual via 6 subdirectories (/en/, /nl/, /de/, /fr/, /es/, /pt/) with hreflang + x-default, with all storage and token math assuming 6 locales per site.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: For the stated target market — small local businesses in Europe — six machine-translated locales per site is an SEO liability, not a feature. A Rotterdam bakery gets five auto-translated copies of the same LocalBusiness content, hreflang-linked, none reviewed by a human. Google explicitly treats bulk auto-translated content without human review as spam, and thin/duplicate localisation at 10,000-site scale is precisely the pattern that attracts a site-level action. It also multiplies token spend, generation latency, R2 object count and the editor's surface area by 6 for pages nobody will visit.
fatal_flaws.correction: Make the locale set a per-tenant choice defaulting to one (the business's own language), with a second locale offered where it is plausible (NL+EN, BE: NL+FR). Keep the fan-out machinery — it is well designed and the marginal-locale story in §3.5 is genuinely the strongest argument for the JSON source of truth — but stop treating 6 as the default. Re-derive the §3.4 storage math and the §4 step-4 cost from a default of 1–2.

fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Nothing is specified for `/`. If the root 301/302s to /nl/, every first-time visitor — including the Lighthouse run and the Googlebot crawl of the homepage — pays an extra round trip on the LCP path and trips the 'Avoid multiple page redirects' audit. For a product whose headline promise is ~100/100, a redirect on the single most-requested URL of every tenant site is a self-inflicted wound.
fatal_flaws.correction: Materialise the default locale at both `/` and `/{defaultLocale}/` with a canonical pointing at one of them and self-referencing hreflang plus x-default on `/`. The cost is one extra object per site per publish, which the §3.4 math shows is free.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.2: 'Zero third-party JS on tenant sites — this is non-negotiable for ~100/100... analytics is the Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon or first-party logging from the renderer — never GA. Total tenant JS budget: < 5 KB gzip, one file, defer.' Plus 'cookie banner is ~1 KB of our own JS'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon is a script loaded from static.cloudflareinsights.com — a third-party origin requiring its own DNS+TLS handshake, and materially larger than the stated total 5 KB budget. Listing it as interchangeable with first-party logging contradicts the 'zero third-party JS' rule in the same paragraph. Separately, a cookie banner that is actually GDPR-compliant for the EU (block-before-consent, granular categories, documented withdrawal) is not 1 KB, and it renders above the fold — that is a CLS risk on the exact viewport Lighthouse measures.
fatal_flaws.correction: Choose first-party logging from the renderer (which you get for free — the renderer already sees every request, and it keeps you out of consent scope entirely) and delete the beacon option. If the site genuinely sets no non-essential cookies and does no cross-site tracking, you may not need a consent banner at all — which is both the better UX and the better CWV outcome. If a banner is required, reserve its space in the layout so it cannot shift content, and re-budget the JS number honestly.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.6: 'the iframe requests preview.mijnsaas.com/{siteId}/{locale}/{path} with a short-lived signed token' and §7 Phase 1 'direct-to-R2 media upload'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Neither is specified securely. A token in the query string leaks via Referer the moment a draft page contains an outbound link (the design mandates a rich footer and a wa.me link on every page), and preview.mijnsaas.com serves unpublished customer content with no noindex mentioned — it sits inside the */* route and is therefore crawlable. Direct-to-R2 upload with no stated presign policy means arbitrary content type and size into a bucket that is later served from a public custom domain: stored XSS and malware hosting under your own brand, with no scanning step anywhere in the pipeline.
fatal_flaws.correction: Put the preview token in a short-lived, HttpOnly, host-scoped cookie set by the app on the preview origin rather than the URL; send `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on every preview response. For uploads, issue server-side presigned PUTs with enforced Content-Type allowlist, Content-Length ceiling and a server-generated key; re-verify the sniffed type after upload; serve media from a separate registrable domain with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and Content-Disposition on anything non-image.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.6: 'editor patches a SiteDraftDO (one Durable Object per site) holding the draft SiteDoc in memory'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Durable Objects hibernate and are evicted; in-memory instance state does not survive that. As written, an editor session that goes idle loses the user's unsaved work — in the product whose entire promise is 'what you see is your site'.
fatal_flaws.correction: Write every patch to DO storage (transactional storage or SQLite-backed DO) and treat memory purely as a read cache rehydrated on constructor. Keep the D1 debounce as designed — that part is right — but the durable copy belongs in DO storage, not in the D1 flush.

missing: Authentication and authorization, entirely. No session design, no cookie scope decision (which is what makes the shared-registrable-domain problem load-bearing), no statement of how the renderer — which is unauthenticated and serves */* — resolves host→siteId without ever trusting a client-supplied siteId, and no tenant→user authorization model in the API or the editor.

Abuse and spend controls: Turnstile or equivalent on onboarding, per-IP/per-account generation quotas, a global concurrency cap on Workflow creation, an Anthropic account spend alert and kill switch, and per-run cost accounting written to generation_runs. Without these the most expensive endpoint in the system is open to the internet.

Stripe specifics that a European SMB product cannot skip: SCA/3DS (mandatory in the EEA and it interacts badly with trial→first-charge 7 days later), webhook idempotency and which Worker owns subscription truth, where the trial-wall is actually enforced (it must be at Workflow dispatch server-side — a disabled 'Regenerate' button in React is not a paywall), VAT/OSS handling on €9,99 across member states, and dunning/failed-renewal behaviour for an annual charge.

GDPR posture for the product itself. The doc rightly refuses to let the model write privacy policies, then never states its own: no DPA/subprocessor list, no data-residency decision. Concretely missing: `inference_geo: "eu"` on the Anthropic calls (supported on the first-party API), D1 location_hint, and — critically — R2 bucket jurisdiction, which is IMMUTABLE after bucket creation. Choosing eu vs default is a genuine one-way door that must be decided before the first bucket exists in Phase 1, and jurisdictional buckets require jurisdiction-specific endpoints, which changes the R2 binding and public-domain setup.

Environments and CI/CD across five deployables: staging vs prod zones, secret provisioning per environment (the doc says use Secrets Store but not how it is wired per env), resource creation ordering (D1/R2/KV/DO namespaces must exist before wrangler deploy), gradual deploys and rollback, and what a preview deployment means for the renderer specifically — which the doc itself notes cannot be tested for cache behaviour under wrangler dev.

Failure and compensation semantics for the generation pipeline. What the user sees when the Workflow fails at step 7 after several dollars of tokens; whether a partial run can resume from the persisted SiteDoc rather than re-generating; how a stuck run is surfaced in the dashboard; and what serves <slug>.mijnsaas.com while generation is in flight or has failed.

Unit economics. There is no cost-per-generation figure, no cost-per-tenant-per-month figure, and no gross-margin check against €119,88 ACV — despite the document making several cost claims (R2 storage, Images, Worker requests). The Cloudflare-for-SaaS line is also missing: 100 custom hostnames are included, then $0.10/hostname/month, i.e. ~$1,000/month at 10,000 custom domains.

Slug namespace management: reservation, collision, profanity/impersonation filtering, squatting, and what happens to <slug>.mijnsaas.com when a tenant churns — all of which are permanent once URLs are indexed and printed.

Accessibility as an engineering constraint rather than a Lighthouse number. The doc promises ~100/100 while also promising AI-chosen per-industry palettes ('dark for a DJ, cream/red for a restaurant'). Contrast ratios are the first thing that breaks. packages/site-kit needs a token-level contrast validator run at publish (and in CI over every archetype × token set), or the a11y score is not reproducible — and Lighthouse's a11y audit is a lint that misses most real failures anyway.
verdict: The spine of this design is right and worth building on: SiteDoc-as-source-of-truth, the disqualification (not merely down-scoring) of raw AI HTML, the renderer as an in-workerd library rather than a per-tenant build step, theming by CSS custom properties instead of a per-site Tailwind pass, D1 for metadata with R2 for bulk, and version-in-the-cache-key so publish is a pointer flip. Its platform facts also survive checking — I verified the 64 MiB uncompressed Worker limit (2026-09-04), wrangler ≥4.34 for the 100k-file/25 MiB asset limits, compatibility_date 2026-08-04 enabling nodejs_compat + v2, 10,000 subrequests (2026-02-11), 6 simultaneous connections, 30s→300s CPU, D1's 10 GB hard cap, Cloudflare for SaaS at 50,000 PAYG hostnames with Enterprise-only wildcards, the Cache API being colo-local and non-tiered, free static-asset requests, and Images at $0.50/1,000 with 5,000 free. That is an unusually high hit rate and the document deserves credit for it. But it is not yet safe to build on, for four reasons that are not stylistic. The routing topology is backwards — Cloudflare's docs say Routes take precedence over Custom Domains, so the */* renderer swallows app, api and marketing, and the doc defers verifying this until Phase 3 even though api ships on a Custom Domain in Phase 1. The most expensive operation in the product (a multi-dollar claude-opus-5 chain) sits behind an unauthenticated public endpoint with no Turnstile, no quota, no concurrency cap and no spend ceiling, against a €119,88 ACV. Two concrete Anthropic API errors sit in the load-bearing snippets: messages.parse() cannot stream, and structured outputs reject recursive schemas and silently strip length/pattern constraints — which falsifies the 'one schema, four consumers, the AI physically cannot emit something the renderer can't draw' keystone. And the security/one-way-door omissions are real: tenant sites share a registrable domain with the authenticated dashboard, and R2 bucket jurisdiction is immutable after creation for a product whose entire market is European SMBs. Fix those four, correct the prompt-cache TTL and layout, add a video encode step (the doc states the requirement and never satisfies it), and re-derive the i18n and Images cost math — then this is a strong Phase 1.
